title: Why Owls Hunt at Night

before.title: Why Owls Hunt at Night
before.text:
Most owls hunt at night. Darkness gives them several advantages when they search for mice and other small animals.

An owl's large eyes gather a great deal of light. The eyes do not move easily inside the head, so the bird turns its neck to change its view. Its ears also help it find prey. In some owls, one ear opening sits higher than the other. A tiny difference in when sound reaches each ear shows where a moving animal is.

Soft edges on the wing feathers reduce the noise of flight. The owl can approach without warning its prey and can still hear sounds below.

These features do not mean that every owl is active only after dark. Some hunt near sunrise or during the day, depending on food and habitat.

Night hunting is therefore not one special ability. It depends on eyes, ears, feathers, and behavior working together in low light.

after.title: Why Owls Hunt at Night
after.text:
Many owl species hunt at night. Their bodies have several features that help them find and catch prey in low light.

Owls have forward-facing eyes and keen eyesight. Their hearing also helps them locate animals that may be difficult to see. Once an owl finds prey, its powerful feet and sharp talons help it catch the animal.

Specialized wing feathers make an owl's flight unusually quiet. Quiet flight helps the bird approach prey, and it also makes it easier for the owl to keep listening while it moves.

Owls do not all hunt in the same way. Some wait on a perch and then glide down. Others search while flying, hover above prey, or even run along the ground. Many hunt close to the ground, where they can see and hear prey more easily.

Most owl species are active at night, but not every owl is nocturnal. Some species are active during the day, while others are most active around dawn and dusk.

reason: Cornell Lab and the Owl Research Institute support the statements about nocturnal activity, eyesight, hearing, talons, specialized feathers and variation among species. Remove the unsupported anatomical detail about uneven ear openings and avoid implying that all owls hunt only at night.

title: Alice at the Mad Tea Party

before.title: Alice at the Mad Tea Party
before.text:
Alice found a long table under a tree. A hare, a man in a large hat, and a sleepy little animal were sitting there.

“There is no room,” they called, although many seats were empty.

Alice sat down anyway.

The conversation became stranger every minute. The man in the hat asked Alice a riddle, but he did not know the answer himself. The hare offered her more tea, even though she had not received any tea yet.

Alice tried to speak politely, but the others kept changing the subject.

Then they explained that time had stopped for them. It was always six o’clock, so it was always tea time. They never finished washing the cups. They simply moved to a clean place at the table.

Alice thought this was a terrible system.

The sleepy animal began telling a story, but the others interrupted him again and again. Soon nobody could remember where the story had begun.

At last Alice stood up.

“This is the strangest tea party I have ever seen,” she said.

She walked away while the others continued talking.

After a few steps, Alice looked back. Nothing had changed. The cups were still moving around the table, and the argument was still going on.

after.title: Alice at the Mad Tea Party
after.text:
Alice found a long table under a tree. The March Hare and the Hatter were having tea, and a sleepy Dormouse sat between them.

“No room!” they cried, although many seats were empty.

Alice sat down anyway. The March Hare offered her wine, but there was no wine on the table. Then the Hatter asked why a raven was like a writing desk. Alice tried to solve the riddle, but the Hatter admitted that he did not know the answer.

The conversation became stranger every minute. The Hatter explained that Time had stopped for him. It was always six o'clock, so it was always tea time. The guests never had time to wash the cups. They simply moved to another place at the table.

The Dormouse began a story about three sisters who lived at the bottom of a well. The Hatter and the March Hare interrupted him, and Alice kept asking questions.

At last, Alice became angry with their rude remarks and walked away. Neither the Hatter nor the March Hare tried to stop her.

“I will never go there again,” Alice said.

Soon she noticed a door in a tree. She entered it and found herself back in the long hall.

title: Alice Plays Croquet with the Queen

before.title: Alice Plays Croquet with the Queen
before.text:
Alice entered a garden where the Queen was preparing to play croquet.

It was not an ordinary game.

The balls were hedgehogs, and the sticks were long birds that moved whenever Alice tried to use them. Even the field was full of holes and bumps.

The Queen took the game very seriously. Whenever something went wrong, she shouted that someone should lose their head.

Most of the players became nervous.

Alice tried to hit her hedgehog, but it walked away. Her bird turned its head and looked at her instead of the ball.

Nearby, the other players were having the same trouble.

The Queen became angrier each minute.

Alice began to realize that nobody was really following the rules. Everyone was too busy watching the Queen and trying not to upset her.

Then the Cheshire Cat appeared above the field. At first, only its smile could be seen.

Alice was glad to have someone familiar to speak with.

The Queen noticed the cat and immediately disliked it.

A new argument began about whether a head without a body could be punished.

Alice quietly stepped away from the game.

She had learned that a game is not much fun when everyone is afraid of the person in charge.

after.title: Alice Plays Croquet with the Queen
after.text:
Alice entered the garden and joined the Queen's game of croquet. It was not an ordinary game.

The balls were live hedgehogs, and the mallets were flamingos. The ground was covered with ridges and holes. The soldiers bent over to make the arches.

Alice tucked a flamingo under her arm, but it kept turning its head to look at her. Whenever she was ready to hit her hedgehog, the animal unrolled itself and crawled away.

All the players took their turns at the same time. They argued and fought over the hedgehogs. The Queen grew furious and kept ordering people to be beheaded.

Alice wondered whether she could escape without being seen. Then a grin appeared in the air. It belonged to the Cheshire Cat, and Alice was glad to have someone familiar to talk to.

The King asked who the cat was. The Queen disliked it and ordered the executioner to cut off its head. This created a problem: only the cat's head could be seen.

The executioner said that he could not cut off a head without a body. The King disagreed. The Queen demanded a quick decision, and Alice suggested asking the Duchess, who owned the cat.

title: Alice Meets the Cheshire Cat

before.title: Alice Meets the Cheshire Cat
before.text:
Alice was walking through the forest when she saw a cat sitting on a branch.

The cat was smiling.

Alice had seen many cats before, but she had never seen one smile like this.

“Which way should I go?” Alice asked.

The cat replied that the answer depended on where she wanted to go.

Alice admitted that she did not really know.

“Then it does not matter which road you take,” said the cat.

This answer did not help very much.

Alice asked who lived nearby. The cat pointed one way and described the strange man with the hat. Then it pointed another way and mentioned the hare.

“They are both mad,” the cat said.

Alice said she did not want to meet mad people.

The cat smiled even more widely. “You cannot avoid that here.”

Before Alice could answer, the cat slowly disappeared.

First its body vanished. Then its head disappeared. The smile remained for a few moments before it was gone too.

Alice stood alone under the tree.

She still did not know which road was best. However, she now understood something about Wonderland: a clear question did not always receive a clear answer.

after.title: Alice Meets the Cheshire Cat
after.text:
Alice was walking through the wood when she saw the Cheshire Cat sitting on a branch. The cat had a wide grin, long claws and many teeth, so Alice spoke to it carefully.

“Which way should I go?” she asked.

The Cat said that the answer depended on where she wanted to go. Alice admitted that she did not care very much.

“Then it does not matter which way you go,” said the Cat. It added that Alice was sure to reach somewhere if she walked long enough.

Alice asked who lived nearby. The Cat pointed one way toward the Hatter and the other way toward the March Hare. It said that both of them were mad.

Alice did not want to meet mad people, but the Cat said that everyone there was mad, including Alice. She did not think its argument proved anything.

The Cat vanished, then appeared again to ask about the baby that had turned into a pig. After Alice answered, it vanished once more.

Soon it returned on another branch. When Alice complained about its sudden movements, the Cat disappeared slowly. Its tail went first, and its grin remained after the rest of it was gone.

reason: Compare the complete retelling with Chapter VI. Restore the Cat’s point that Alice will reach somewhere if she walks long enough, its claim that Alice is mad too, and the two-stage disappearance in which it first vanishes and later fades slowly from tail to grin.
